question_interpretation: Contrast what Part 111 requires of quality control (QC) personnel with what it requires of the personnel who manufacture, package, label or hold dietary supplements.

issues.detail: 'QC independence' is not a Part 111 requirement. Part 111 has no word 'independent' or 'independence'. QC personnel may be 'within or outside of your organization' (111.3), and under 111.12(b) a person may perform both QC and other operations as long as the QC responsibilities are 'distinct and separate'. The 2007 preamble (72 FR 34800, 34810) says QC need not be a distinct or separate unit or person, and QC personnel 'can have dual functions'.

'No self-approval of own work' does not appear in Part 111 for QC review. The preamble (72 FR 34800) gives an example of a packaging expert who does packaging QC and also works in the packaging operation. The only two-person verification rule is in the MMR/BPR for weighing, measuring and adding components in manual operations (111.210(h)(3)(ii); 111.260(j)(2)). That rule is about production steps, not QC approval.

J does not list the QC duties that the question asks for: approve or reject processes, specifications, procedures, controls, tests and deviations (111.105(a)); review supplier-qualification and specification-basis documentation (111.105(b)-(e)); ensure representative and reserve samples are collected (111.105(f)-(g)); conduct all material reviews and disposition decisions (111.87, 111.113); approve and release or reject batches (111.123). J also does not state the production-side requirements: qualified employees with education, training or experience (111.12(a),(c)) and qualified supervisors (111.13).

G names 111.105 and 111.12 but leaves out 111.87 (QC alone makes material review and disposition decisions) and 111.3 (QC personnel may be inside or outside the firm). These are central to the distinction.

explanation: 111.105 and 111.12 are the right core sections. Two of the four key elements, 'QC independence' and 'no self-approval of own work', are not in the regulation. The text requires only that each QC person be qualified and keep QC responsibilities 'distinct and separate' from their other duties. The QC personnel definition expressly allows QC to sit inside or outside the organization. A correct answer that says Part 111 does not require an independent QC unit would contradict this key.
proposed_corrected_answer: QC personnel (any person or group, inside or outside the firm, that you designate; 111.3) must be identified and qualified. When performing QC, they must hold responsibilities 'distinct and separate' from any other duties they have (111.12(b)). Part 111 does not require an independent QC unit, and one person may hold both roles. QC personnel must ensure that operations ensure product quality and that packaging and labeling match the MMR. They approve or reject processes, specifications, written procedures, controls, tests and deviations; review and approve supplier-qualification and specification-basis documentation; ensure representative and reserve samples are collected; and determine whether specifications are met (111.105). QC alone conducts material reviews and makes disposition decisions (111.87; 111.113) and approves, releases or rejects batches (111.123). Production personnel must be qualified employees with the education, training or experience for their assigned functions (111.12(a),(c)), under qualified supervisors (111.13). They carry out operations according to the MMR and BPR.

question_interpretation: What Part 111 requires for incoming components, packaging and labels before they are used in manufacture: receipt examination, quarantine, sampling, specification verification (identity/COA), QC approval and release, lot identification, holding, and handling of rejected materials.

issues.detail: The identity-verification and COA-reliance elements in J come from 111.75(a)(1)-(2), not from 111.155 or 111.160. The pre-use packaging and label checks are in 111.75(f). Rejection of unsuitable materials is in 111.77 and 111.170. QC pre-use operations are in 111.120. G cites none of these, so an answer that cites the provisions actually governing J's elements may be scored as off-key.

J leaves out requirements stated in the cited sections: visual examination of containers (content label, damage, broken seals) and of the supplier invoice, guarantee or certification (111.155(a)-(b), 111.160(a)-(b)); collection of representative samples; QC review and approval of results and release from quarantine (111.155(c), 111.160(c)); unique lot identification and traceability (111.155(d), 111.160(d)); and holding conditions (111.155(e), 111.160(e)).

'Identity verification of each component' is imprecise. A dietary ingredient needs at least one identity test or examination unless FDA grants a petition exemption (111.75(a)(1)). The identity of other components may be confirmed by testing or by a qualified supplier COA (111.75(a)(2)). Packaging and labels need, at minimum, a visual identification or examination plus review of the supplier invoice, guarantee or certification (111.75(f)).

explanation: The key's themes are real requirements (identity, COA conditions, quarantine, rejection). But two of the four elements come from sections G does not cite (111.75, 111.170), and J leaves out most of what 111.155 and 111.160 require: receipt examination, sampling, QC release from quarantine, lot traceability and holding. An answer complete for the question needs 111.75(a) and (f), 111.120 and 111.170 alongside 111.155 and 111.160.
proposed_corrected_answer: On receipt, visually examine containers for appropriate content label, damage or broken seals, and the supplier's invoice, guarantee or certification against the purchase order (111.155(a)-(b); 111.160(a)-(b)). Quarantine until representative samples are collected (for packaging and labels, with at least a visual identification of containers and closures), QC has reviewed and approved any test or examination results, and QC has approved the material and released it from quarantine (111.155(c); 111.160(c); 111.120). Verify specifications before use (111.75): for a dietary ingredient, at least one appropriate identity test or examination, unless FDA grants a 111.75(a)(1)(ii) petition exemption; for other components, confirm identity and other 111.70(b) specifications by testing or by a supplier COA under the 111.75(a)(2)(ii) conditions; for packaging and labels, at least a visual identification or examination plus review of the supplier's invoice, guarantee or certification (111.75(f)). Give each unique lot a traceable identifier (111.155(d); 111.160(d)). Hold materials so as to prevent contamination, deterioration and mixups (111.155(e); 111.160(e)). QC must reject nonconforming material (111.77), and rejected material must be identified, held and controlled under a quarantine system (111.170). Records go under 111.180.

question_interpretation: Whether a manufacturer may rely on a supplier certificate of analysis instead of its own identity testing of a component. The answer differs for dietary ingredients and other components.

issues.detail: J says the manufacturer is required to test dietary-ingredient identity but leaves out the exception in the same paragraph G cites: a firm may petition FDA under 21 CFR 10.30 (111.75(a)(1)(ii)), and if FDA grants the petition, it tests under the terms FDA specifies.

J lists only supplier qualification and periodic re-confirmation. It leaves out the other mandatory COA conditions: the COA must describe the test methods, limits and actual results (111.75(a)(2)(ii)(B)); the firm must keep documentation of how it qualified the supplier (C); and QC personnel must review and approve the qualification documentation (E).

COA reliance covers confirming the identity of non-dietary-ingredient components as well as their other specifications (111.75(a)(2)). 'Other component specs' should say so. 111.155 (receipt and quarantine) is only a minor fit; 111.95(b)(2) (records of supplier qualification) and 111.105(b) (QC approval) are more relevant.

explanation: The core rule is correct and correctly cited at 111.75(a)(1)-(2). Identity testing of a dietary ingredient cannot be replaced by a COA, while other components may rely on a COA under conditions. J leaves out the petition exemption in 111.75(a)(1)(ii), which goes to whether the practice is 'allowed', and three of the five COA conditions.
proposed_corrected_answer: It depends on the component. For a dietary ingredient, no: the firm must conduct at least one appropriate test or examination to verify identity before use (111.75(a)(1)(i)). The only alternative is a 21 CFR 10.30 petition showing no material diminution of assurance; if FDA grants it, the firm tests under the terms FDA specifies (111.75(a)(1)(ii)). For any other component, the firm may confirm identity and other 111.70(b) specifications through a supplier COA, but only if it first qualifies the supplier by confirming the supplier's test results; the COA describes the test methods, limits and actual results; the firm documents how it qualified the supplier; it periodically re-confirms the COA; and QC reviews and approves the qualification and re-qualification basis (111.75(a)(2)(ii)(A)-(E); 111.105(b); records under 111.95(b)(2)).

question_interpretation: List the contents Part 111 requires in a master manufacturing record.

issues.detail: J leaves out several items 111.210 enumerates: a statement of any intentional overage of a dietary ingredient (111.210(e)); a statement of theoretical yield at each control point and at completion, with the maximum and minimum percentages beyond which a deviation investigation and material review are needed (111.210(f)); procedures for sampling and a cross-reference to test procedures (h)(2); specific actions to perform and verify control points, including weight or measure verification and, for manual operations, one person weighing or adding a component and a second person verifying ((h)(3)); special notations and precautions ((h)(4)); and corrective action plans ((h)(5)).

'Batch size' is not a separate content item. 111.210(a) requires strength, concentration, weight or measure of each dietary ingredient 'for each batch size', and 111.205(a) requires an MMR for each batch size. 'In-process controls' is a loose summary of (h)(1) and (h)(3).

explanation: G is the right section. J reflects items (a)-(d), (g) and part of (h) but leaves out the overage statement, the theoretical yield limits that trigger deviation investigations, the two-person verification for manual operations, and corrective action plans. These are distinct enumerated requirements, so J is incomplete for a 'what must it include' question.
proposed_corrected_answer: Under 111.210 the MMR must include: (a) the supplement name and the strength, concentration, weight or measure of each dietary ingredient for each batch size; (b) a complete list of components; (c) an accurate statement of the weight or measure of each component; (d) the identity and weight or measure of each dietary ingredient declared on the Supplement Facts label, and the identity of each ingredient on the ingredient list; (e) any intentional overage of a dietary ingredient; (f) theoretical yield at each control point and at completion, with maximum and minimum percentages beyond which deviation investigation and material review are required; (g) a description of packaging and a representative label (or a cross-reference to it); and (h) written instructions covering specifications for each control point, sampling procedures with a cross-reference to test procedures, specific actions to perform and verify each control point (including weight or measure and addition verification, with a second-person check for manual operations), special notations and precautions, and corrective action plans.

These are central, enumerated BPR contents.

question_interpretation: What the laboratory control processes required by Part 111 must include (Subpart J).

issues.detail: 21 CFR 111.310 is 'What are the requirements for the laboratory facilities that you use?' (adequate laboratory facilities). Laboratory control processes are governed by 21 CFR 111.315, 'What are the requirements for laboratory control processes?'. A correct answer citing 111.315 would fail citation-exact against this key.

'Criteria for accepting/rejecting test results' is not an element of 111.315. The section lists criteria for establishing appropriate specifications, sampling plans, criteria for selecting examination and testing methods, criteria for selecting standard reference materials, and use of test methods in accordance with established criteria. 'Sample use' does not match any listed item.

J leaves out: criteria for establishing appropriate specifications (111.315(a)); criteria for selecting standard reference materials (d); use of test methods and examinations in accordance with established criteria (e); the five categories that sampling plans must cover (b)(1)-(5); and the responsible party, since the processes must be reviewed and approved by QC personnel (111.315 intro; 111.110(a)).

explanation: The key cites the laboratory-facilities section (111.310) instead of 111.315, which governs laboratory control processes. Its element list includes an item not in the regulation ('criteria for accepting/rejecting test results') and leaves out three of the five enumerated items and the QC approval requirement. Only 'sampling plans' and 'criteria for selecting test methods' are supported.
proposed_corrected_answer: You must establish and follow laboratory control processes that are reviewed and approved by quality control personnel (111.315; see also 111.110(a)). They must include: (a) use of criteria for establishing appropriate specifications; (b) use of sampling plans for obtaining representative samples, in accordance with Subpart E, of components, packaging and labels; in-process materials; finished batches; product received for packaging or labeling; and packaged and labeled dietary supplements; (c) use of criteria for selecting appropriate examination and testing methods; (d) use of criteria for selecting standard reference materials; and (e) use of test methods and examinations in accordance with established criteria. Related: written laboratory procedures (111.303), adequate laboratory facilities (111.310), and records (111.325).

question_interpretation: What Part 111 requires of the laboratory methods used for testing and examination.

issues.detail: 'Verification of suitability for the matrix' paraphrases beyond the text. 111.320(a) requires verifying that methodologies are 'appropriate for their intended use'; Part 111 never uses the word 'matrix'. Matrix suitability is one reasonable reading of 'intended use', but a grader looking for 'matrix' could mark down a verbatim-correct answer.

111.75(h) also governs test and examination methods. They must be appropriate, scientifically valid methods and must include at least one of: gross organoleptic, macroscopic, microscopic or chemical analysis, or another scientifically valid method. G does not cite 111.75(h). Related: written procedures for tests (111.303), documentation that methodology is followed, with results (111.325(b)(2)), and QC review and approval of laboratory control processes, including method-selection criteria (111.315(c); 111.110).

111.320(b) requires identifying and using a scientifically valid method 'for each established specification for which testing or examination is required'. J's 'methods must be appropriate and scientifically valid' captures this only loosely.

explanation: 111.320 is the right core section, and J's 'appropriate and scientifically valid' element is supported. But J substitutes 'suitability for the matrix' for the regulatory 'appropriate for their intended use', and it leaves out the parallel method requirements in 111.75(h), including the list of acceptable method types.

question_interpretation: What Part 111 requires of manufacturing operations to prevent contamination (Subpart K).

issues.detail: J's 'sanitation' element comes from 111.360 ('You must conduct all manufacturing operations in accordance with adequate sanitation principles'), which G does not cite. 111.370 (rejected supplements held under quarantine) and 111.353 (written procedures) are also Subpart K requirements.

J is too generic to measure completeness against 111.365. It does not name the enumerated precautions: protective conditions and controls; washing components that contain soil; water quality; testing to prevent use of contaminated components; microbial controls (sterilizing, pH, aw, etc.); holding of materials that support rapid microbial growth; segregating material under review; contamination controls for mechanical steps; protection against metal or foreign material (filters, magnets, metal detectors); and identifying batch containers, processing lines and major equipment.

explanation: 111.365 is the right primary section and nothing in J is wrong. But J's sanitation element comes from the uncited 111.360, and J's three high-level themes do not capture the eleven enumerated precautions, so the key cannot tell a complete answer from a vague one.
proposed_corrected_answer: Conduct all manufacturing operations under adequate sanitation principles (111.360) and take all necessary precautions to prevent contamination (111.365). These include: (a) conditions and controls against microbial growth and contamination; (b) washing or cleaning components with soil or other contaminants; (c) using water that meets Federal, State and local requirements when it may become a component; (d) chemical, microbiological or other testing as necessary to prevent use of contaminated components; (e) sterilizing, pasteurizing, freezing, refrigerating, controlling pH, humidity or water activity, or other effective means against microorganisms and decomposition; (f) holding materials that can support rapid growth of pathogens so as to prevent adulteration; (g) identifying and holding materials under material review apart from others; (h) protecting mechanical steps (cleaning and sanitizing contact surfaces, temperature and time controls); (i) effective measures against metal or other foreign material (filters, traps, magnets, metal detectors); (j) segregating and identifying batch containers; and (k) identifying processing lines and major equipment with contents and batch. Rejected supplements must be held under a quarantine system (111.370).

question_interpretation: What Part 111 requires for packaging and labeling operations (Subpart L).

issues.detail: 'Gang printing controls' is not a Part 111 requirement. Part 111 contains no gang-printing provision. That requirement is drug CGMP, 21 CFR 211.122(f). A correct Part 111 answer would not mention it.

J lists label reconciliation without the 111.410(b) exception: reconciliation is not required for cut or rolled labels if a 100-percent examination for correct labels is performed by appropriate electronic or electromechanical equipment.

J and G leave out: repackaging and relabeling only after QC approval, with sampling and QC batch approval (111.420); quarantine of rejected packaged and labeled product (111.425); written procedures (111.403); assigning lot numbers and examining representative samples against 111.70(g) (111.415(f)-(g)); disposing of obsolete or incorrect labels (111.415(h)); traceability through distribution (111.410(d)); and QC operations for packaging and labeling (111.127).

explanation: 111.410 and 111.415 are the right core sections, and most J themes are supported. But 'gang printing controls' imports a drug-CGMP requirement (21 CFR 211.122(f)) that does not exist in Part 111. That is a requirement-that-does-not-exist error. J also leaves out the reconciliation exception and the repackaging/relabeling and rejection rules in 111.420 and 111.425.
proposed_corrected_answer: Determine whether packaging meets specifications (111.410(a)). Control the issuance and use of packaging and labels and reconcile discrepancies; reconciliation is not required for cut or rolled labels when 100% electronic or electromechanical label examination is performed (111.410(b)). Examine packaging and labels for each batch before operations to confirm conformity to the MMR (111.410(c)). Be able to determine the complete manufacturing history through distribution (111.410(d)). Fill, assemble, package and label so as to ensure quality and conformance to the MMR, including cleaning and sanitizing equipment and packaging, protecting against airborne contamination, sanitary handling, physical or spatial separation to prevent mixups, identifying unlabeled filled containers, assigning lot numbers, examining a representative sample of each batch against 111.70(g), and disposing of obsolete or incorrect labels and packaging (111.415). Repackage or relabel only with QC approval, with sampling and QC batch approval (111.420). Quarantine rejected packaged and labeled product (111.425). Follow written procedures (111.403), and QC performs the 111.127 operations. Part 111 has no gang-printing provision.

question_interpretation: What Part 111 requires for holding and distributing dietary supplements and related materials (Subpart M).

issues.detail: J's distribution element ('distribution under conditions protecting against deterioration') is governed by 111.470, which G does not cite. G also leaves out 111.460 (holding in-process material) and 111.475 (records, including records of product distribution).

J does not give the specific conditions: temperature, humidity and light for components and supplements; conditions preventing mixup, contamination and deterioration (111.455); and, for reserve samples, conditions consistent with the product label (or ordinary storage), the same container-closure system, and retention for 1 year past the shelf-life date or 2 years from distribution of the last associated batch (111.465).
The holding requirements do not apply to dietary supplements held at a retail establishment solely for direct retail sale to individual consumers (111.1(b)).

explanation: 111.453, 111.455 and 111.465 are correct, and J's themes are supported. But the distribution element is governed by 111.470, which G omits. G also omits 111.460 and 111.475, and J leaves out the reserve-sample retention period and container-closure requirements.
proposed_corrected_answer: Establish and follow written procedures for holding and distributing (111.453). Hold components and dietary supplements under appropriate temperature, humidity and light so identity, purity, strength and composition are not affected; hold packaging and labels so they are not adversely affected; and hold all of them under conditions that prevent mixup, contamination and deterioration (111.455). Identify and hold in-process material under protective conditions of temperature, humidity and light (111.460). Hold reserve samples under label-consistent (or ordinary) storage conditions in the same container-closure system, and retain them for 1 year past the shelf-life date (if used) or 2 years from distribution of the last associated batch (111.465). Distribute under conditions protecting against contamination and deterioration (111.470). Keep written procedures and distribution records (111.475). The holding requirements do not apply to retail establishments holding product solely for direct retail sale to individual consumers (111.1(b)).

question_interpretation: What Part 111 requires a manufacturer to do when a distributor returns a dietary supplement (Subpart N).

issues.detail: J includes 'investigation of other batches', but that requirement is in 111.530, which G does not cite.

J states the investigation without its condition. 111.530 applies only 'If the reason for a dietary supplement being returned implicates other batches', and it extends to the manufacturing processes as well as those batches.

Not listed: the material review is mandatory because the product was returned (111.113(a)(5)); QC operations for returns (111.130); written procedures (111.503); and records (111.535). 'Destruction or reprocessing conditions' should state the default: destroy or suitably dispose of the product unless QC approves salvage for redistribution or reprocessing (111.515). Reprocessed returns must meet all 111.70(e) specifications, and QC approves or rejects their release (111.525).

explanation: The cited sections 111.510-111.525 are correct and support quarantine, QC material review, the destroy-unless-approved rule, salvage and reprocessing. But the investigation element comes from the uncited 111.530 and is stated without its trigger (the return reason implicates other batches). The key also leaves out 111.113(a)(5) and 111.535.
proposed_corrected_answer: Identify and quarantine the returned supplement until QC conducts a material review and makes a disposition decision (111.510; 111.113(a)(5); 111.130). Destroy or otherwise suitably dispose of it unless QC approves salvage for redistribution or approves reprocessing (111.515). Salvage only if QC's material review and disposition decision allows it (111.520). Any reprocessed return must meet all 111.70(e) product specifications, and QC approves or rejects its release (111.525). If the reason for the return implicates other batches, investigate the manufacturing processes and each of those batches for compliance with specifications (111.530). Follow written procedures (111.503) and keep records of the material review and disposition, test results and QC reevaluation (111.535).

question_interpretation: What a firm must do on receiving a product complaint about a dietary supplement. The domain is Part 111 (Subpart O), though the question does not say so.

issues.detail: Under 111.560(a), a 'qualified person' reviews all product complaints and investigates those involving a possible failure. QC personnel's role (111.560(b); 111.135) is to review and approve the decision whether to investigate, and the investigation's findings and followup. J's 'QC personnel review' blurs these two roles.

J's 'record required information' element comes from 111.570, which G does not cite. 111.570 requires a written record of every complaint related to good manufacturing practice, including the product name and description, lot number (if available), date received and complainant contact (if available), nature of the complaint, any reply, and investigation findings and followup.

J leaves out 111.560(c): the review, investigation and QC review must extend to all relevant batches and records. J also does not say that investigation is required only for complaints involving a possible failure to meet specifications or other Part 111 requirements, including those that may result in a risk of illness or injury.

Outside Part 111: if the complaint reports a serious adverse event, the responsible person (the manufacturer, packer or distributor named on the label) must report it to FDA within 15 business days and keep adverse-event records for 6 years (FD&C Act 761, 21 U.S.C. 379aa-1). This matters if the question is read as asking about all obligations rather than Part 111 only.

explanation: 111.553 and 111.560 are the right core sections, and the review/possible-failure/investigate sequence is supported. But J assigns the initial review to QC when the rule assigns it to a qualified person, its recordkeeping element rests on the uncited 111.570, and it leaves out the all-relevant-batches-and-records requirement.
proposed_corrected_answer: Follow written complaint procedures (111.553). A qualified person must review every product complaint to determine whether it involves a possible failure to meet specifications or other Part 111 requirements, including those that could result in a risk of illness or injury, and must investigate any complaint that does (111.560(a)). QC personnel must review and approve the decision whether to investigate and the findings and followup of any investigation (111.560(b); 111.135). The review and investigation must extend to all relevant batches and records (111.560(c)). Keep a written record of every GMP-related complaint, made at the time of performance, with the product name and description, lot number (if available), date received and complainant contact (if available), nature of the complaint, any reply, and investigation findings and followup (111.570). If the complaint is a serious adverse event, the responsible person named on the label must also report it to FDA within 15 business days under FD&C Act 761 (21 U.S.C. 379aa-1).

question_interpretation: How long Part 111 records must be kept, and how they must be kept and made available to FDA (Subpart P).

issues.detail: J says the retention period is 'tied to date of manufacture/expiration' and gives no figures. 111.605(a) ties retention to the shelf-life date (1 year past it, if shelf-life dating is used) or to distribution (2 years beyond the date of distribution of the last batch associated with the records). The date of manufacture plays no part, and J omits both numbers.
J says 'original or true copy' but leaves out the third permitted form, electronic records, and the rule that all electronic records must comply with 21 CFR Part 11 (111.605(b)-(c)).

On availability, J leaves out that records (or copies) must be 'readily available during the retention period' 'when requested' (111.610(a)), and that firms using reduction techniques such as microfilming must make suitable reader and photocopying equipment readily available to FDA (111.610(b)). The responsible party is 'you', the person subject to Part 111.

explanation: G cites the governing sections. But J's central retention element is wrong: it anchors retention to the date of manufacture, while 111.605(a) sets 1 year past the shelf-life date or 2 years beyond distribution of the last associated batch. J gives neither figure, and it leaves out electronic records with Part 11 compliance and the reader/photocopier requirement.
proposed_corrected_answer: Keep all records required by Part 111 for 1 year past the shelf-life date, if shelf-life dating is used, or 2 years beyond the date of distribution of the last batch of dietary supplements associated with those records (111.605(a)). Records may be kept as originals, as true copies (photocopies, microfilm, microfiche or other accurate reproductions), or as electronic records; electronic records must comply with 21 CFR Part 11 (111.605(b)-(c)). All required records, or copies, must be readily available during the retention period for inspection and copying by FDA when requested (111.610(a)). If reduction techniques such as microfilming are used, suitable reader and photocopying equipment must be readily available to FDA (111.610(b)).
